title: Content (Philippians 4:11–13)
hookLine: I have learned to be content, and I can do all things in him

lines: I CAN DO ALL THINGS: ON A GYM SHIRT.
READ IN PLACE: A THANK-YOU NOTE.
A GIFT SENT TO A PRISONER.
cards: I can do all things. It turns up on gym shirts, on locker-room walls, under an athlete's eyes in black grease paint.
There it reads like a promise of winning: with God's help I'll make the team, close the deal, run the marathon. Read in place, it's something quieter. It comes near the end of a thank-you note.
The church at Philippi had sent Paul a gift in prison, carried by a friend named Epaphroditus. And Paul, thanking them, says something surprising about needing it.

teach.h: NOT AS IT WERE FOR WANT.
teach.b: He's glad of the gift, but he doesn't want them to think he was desperate: "Not as it were for want. For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Then he names the states.
He knows how to be brought low and how to abound; to be full and to be hungry; to have plenty and to go without. And he says he's been instructed in all of it.
The Greek word is the one used for being initiated into a secret. Paul has learned the secret of being content. Then: "I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me."
All things, here, means both: hunger and plenty, prison and freedom. Not winning, but standing steady through either. The word for content is autarkēs, and it's borrowed.
It was an ideal the Stoic and Cynic philosophers prized: self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul takes their word and changes its center.
Not sufficient in myself, but sufficient in him.
And notice the first verb: I have learned. Contentment, for Paul, isn't a personality type. It's a skill, and it took practice, and he learned it in some very hard places.
Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment speaks of the same freedom: a heart that isn't ruled by envy or by the need for more, which the Catechism calls poverty of heart.

teach.h: I CAN DO ALL THINGS IN HIM WHO STRENGTHENETH ME.
teach.b: And Paul doesn't despise the gift either. He calls it a sweet fragrance, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Content doesn't mean ungrateful.
It means grateful, without being owned.

how: Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment commends "poverty of heart" and freedom from envy and greed; Catholics practice contentment through simplicity, fasting and almsgiving.

o: happy because everything is going your way
steady in hunger or plenty, sufficient in him
needing nothing and no one but yourself

games.q: inside the thank-you note — tap the pairs.

s: 'I can do all things' is about winning
it's about standing steady in both hunger and plenty.
the verse comes from a thank-you note for a gift
the Philippians sent Paul help in prison.
Paul says he was born content

games.q: you're in prison, and your friends have sent you a gift. how do you thank them?
o: say you were desperate and ask for more.
say you've learned to be content in plenty or want, and thank them warmly.
say you never needed anything from anyone.
games.why: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith," and he calls their gift a sweet fragrance.

practice: Look around wherever you are and quietly name five things that are here: a chair holding you up, light, your breath, a sound, a person or the memory of one.
Don't name what's missing; let what's here be enough, and if a want shows up, let it pass by. If you pray, say today's verse slowly; if not, simply rest in what's already here.

wordCard.voice: Content. Paul's word from prison: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content, because I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: self-sufficient, content; a Stoic ideal that Paul re-centers 'in him' (Philippians 4:11).

carryVoice: Your line: I have learned. Contentment is a skill, not a mood. See you tomorrow.
